summary: For 9–11s: rainforests regulate climate in two linked ways — a growing tree pulls CO2 from the air and locks the carbon into its wood (a carbon store or 'sink'), and transpiration from the leaves supplies water vapour that feeds regional rainfall. The decisive insight is that the SAME forest flips roles: standing, it holds carbon out of the air and helps make rain; burned or cleared, it releases that stored carbon back as CO2 (quickly if burned, more slowly as cleared wood decays) and less rain is recycled. Clearing is a 'double hit' — lost future absorption plus released past storage. Build on prior water-cycle and deforestation learning, and correct the 'lungs of the planet / makes our oxygen' myth by redirecting to carbon storage and rainfall.
misconceptions: 'Rainforests are the lungs of the Earth / make most of our oxygen' — net oxygen contribution is small; their climate value is carbon storage and rainfall.
'A forest only matters while it's growing' — an intact mature forest is a huge carbon STORE, and burning it releases that store.
'Cutting trees just removes shade' — it releases stored carbon and disrupts regional rainfall.
'CO2 from forests is separate from climate change' — forest carbon is part of the same atmospheric CO2 that warms the planet.
'Replanting instantly cancels the carbon released' — regrowth takes decades to re-store the carbon lost in seconds of burning.

activities.title: Run the forest's carbon budget both ways
steps: Study a single forest with four coupled dials overhead: CO2 in the air, carbon locked in the trees, regional rainfall, and temperature.
Let the forest grow and observe the flows: the air-CO2 dial sinks, carbon piles into the wood, rainfall stays lush, temperature holds steady — describe aloud what role the forest is playing.

Trigger a 'burn/clear' action and watch stored carbon go back into the air: the CO2 dial rises, temperature ticks up, and because the transpiring leaves are gone, the rainfall dial slides lower (the dials show the direction of each effect over time in a simplified model, not a calibrated amount; one real forest alone would not visibly move global temperature).
State in your own words how the SAME forest played two opposite roles, and why that connects a distant forest to the whole planet's climate.
activities.insight: An intact forest is a carbon store (and usually a sink) and helps make rain; burning or clearing it reverses both — releasing stored carbon as CO2 (worsening warming) and reducing transpiration-driven rainfall. The forest is a two-way climate regulator.

activities.title: Trace the carbon-cycle arrows on a reveal diagram
steps: Explore a carbon-cycle diagram with arrows: CO2 in via photosynthesis, carbon stored in wood, CO2 out via burning and respiration.
Reveal the tree to read 'absorbs CO2, stores carbon in wood'; reveal a fire to read 'releases it back as CO2'.
Compare a before/after panel of the same forest intact versus burned, noting where the stored carbon goes.
Say which arrow is bigger when a forest is standing and which is bigger when it is burned (remember respiration releases some CO2 even from a standing forest).
activities.insight: Learners name the mechanism and vocabulary: photosynthesis moves carbon from air into wood; respiration and decay always return some as CO2, and burning returns large amounts quickly. The forest is a sink when uptake is bigger than release and a source when release is bigger, as happens when it is burned.

activities.title: Explain and sequence the deforestation chain
steps: Complete the statement: an intact rainforest acts as a carbon ____ (sink).
State what is released into the atmosphere when a forest is burned, and where that carbon had been stored.
Put the steps in order: forest cleared/burned → stored carbon released as CO2 → more CO2 in the atmosphere → global temperatures rise.
Answer: if a country replants a forest, does that instantly cancel the carbon released when the old one burned? Explain why or why not.
Answer: how could losing a rainforest change rainfall far away, not just the local temperature?
activities.insight: Learners can state the sink idea, the carbon-release-on-burning mechanism, the deforestation→CO2→warming chain, and transfer the two-way idea to new cases (regrowth takes decades; less transpiration can reduce rainfall in regions far off).

activities.title: Bust the 'lungs of the planet' myth
steps: Respond to the claim: 'Rainforests matter for climate mainly because they make most of the oxygen we breathe.' Decide whether this is the main reason, and explain why.
Explain what else in a mature forest uses up oxygen (plants and soil organisms respire; decay consumes oxygen too), so its net oxygen output is small.
State the two real climate roles: carbon storage (a sink) and transpiration-driven rainfall.
Consider that scientists think much of Earth's oxygen comes from ocean phytoplankton, not from rainforests — another reason the 'lungs' slogan is misleading.
activities.insight: The 'lungs/oxygen' slogan is misleading because a mature forest's NET oxygen output is small; the real climate importance is carbon storage and rainfall, and the same forest becomes a carbon source when burned.

checkQuestion: People often call rainforests 'the lungs of the planet' and say they matter for climate mainly because they make most of the oxygen we breathe. Is that the main reason rainforests matter to the climate? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: No — the 'lungs / makes most of our oxygen' idea is a myth. A mature rainforest uses up almost as much oxygen as it makes (plants and soil organisms respire, and decay consumes oxygen too), so its NET oxygen output is small; most of Earth's oxygen actually comes from ocean plankton. The real climate importance is different: rainforests are a huge CARBON STORE — they lock enormous amounts of carbon in their wood and soil, so they act as a carbon sink — and their transpiration recycles water that drives rainfall regionally and beyond. Crucially, when the SAME forest is burned or cleared, that stored carbon is released as CO2, flipping the forest from a sink into a SOURCE that warms the climate.
